speechtext: And even 17 per cent.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Indeed, even 17 per cent, as the Hon. Member for Mississauga South just said. Why would the students at Loyalist College in the Belleville area support this Bill? These students are attending the only course in North America-not just in Hastings County, not just in Ontario, not just in Canada, but in North America-where they can learn to handle the new Government technology on Telidon. We saw in the newspapers the other day that the federal Government will now spend $24 million in advertising the new Telidon technology, yet when those yound people graduate from that course, well-trained in this technology, there is not a job to be found. Out of the first course about half of the students found employment; out of the second, none; and the third course is now going in and there are no jobs to handle this technology.
Why would marina operators advocate my support of this Bill? In my area there is a tremendous tourist industry, yet there is a marina operator on the north shore of Prince Edward County who asked for a small business investment grant, a program of this Government, but was told he could not have it because he, very wisely as a businessman, wanted to buy only good used equipment. No, he could not have it for that; he would have to buy new equipment. Why would he want me to support this Bill? Another businessman who was interested in a small craft harbours grant to open the entrance to his harbour was told in 1980 that he would have it in 1982. In 1982 he was told that he may have it in 1985-86. Why would tourist operators or marina operators in my constituency want me to support this Bill?
Why would the truckers in this area want me to support this Bill? After all, Maislin Transport received a shot in the arm of some $34 million a short while ago. None of the trucking companies in my constituency, no matter how hardpressed they are for work or how many employees they have laid off, are receiving any support from the federal Government.
I could go on and on and on, but my time is running out. I just named a few people in my area who might benefit by the largesse of the federal Government, which will spend on behalf of those people $250 million in ordinary spending and some $80 million in deficit spending. It seems to me that there is little or no justification for this when the people of Prince Edward-Hastings cannot benefit from it. I will tell the House who benefits from it. It is the friends of the federal Government. If this Party digs in its heels and asks for some real accounting on this Bill, it will be true justice.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join my colleagues in the House of Commons today to speak to the amendment to Bill C-143, a Bill to borrow $19 billion. In particular I am speaking to the amendment which requests that the Bill go to committee so that the Members of the House, the people of Canada and I will know what is going on
February 28, 1983

at this historic moment. As many speakers have pointed out today, not since Confederation has the Government of Canada sought to borrow so much money at one time.
Some of my colleagues on this side of the House who have spoken today attempted, and reasonably so, to show to the people of Canada and to Members of Parliament what $19 billion means. The Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) just attempted to do that. In all honesty I must say that I just do not understand the magnitude of $19 billion. We have come to a time in our history in which our debt has grown to such a degree that at present we cannot possibly imagine what is happening. This to me has become totally unreasonable. In taking the unreasonable amount of $19 billion the Government does not show what it is going to do with that money, which makes the situation completely unreasonable.
I come to the basic problem. It is happening to us here in the House of Commons and it is affecting the people of Canada. People have lost credibility in the process of Parliament. This past week, while I was knocking on doors in my own constituency, a remark was made very frequently to me. I am sure if other Hon. Members were doing the same thing, they would hear the same remark. I was asked, "What are your gooks doing in the House of Commons?" That is a very serious question. The very phrasing of it means that people have lost credibility about what is going on here. It is important that this borrowing Bill go to committee and be made public so that people will know what the $19 billion is all about.
Some reasonableness must be attached to this. If there is no reasonableness, and with the power of television looking in on us, it is no wonder people ask, "What are you gooks doing?" We moved this amendment because I think it is a reasonable and an honest thing for Canadians and for people in this House to know more about what is happening. Canada is falling into what is known as the debt trap in the international world. This trap is one which countries fall into and from which they can no longer get out. Then they collapse.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is socialism. That is what it is.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The situation happens very rapidly. There are countries which had strong economies five and six years ago- or at least were giving the appearance of being strong-but as a result of international events that have taken place during that time they have collapsed or are collapsing. Basically, the situation is called a debt trap. Countries falling into this debt trap have debts that get higher and higher. Finally, the debt controls their life, their economy and their history.
I repeat again that this House has to become credible. This Government has to be responsible. This House must show that what is taking place here is not taking this country into the debt trap.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
In the last several months in Canada events have taken place which point to the lack of credibility about which I
Borrowing Authority
am speaking. The Social Action Committee of the Canadian Catholic Bishops issued a statement at the beginning of January which, as far as I know, probably had as much effect in the media and in discussions in Canada about our economy than any other statement ever issued by the Catholic or any other church group in Canada. The statement issued by the Bishops discussed the same theme that I am discussing now. It is the ethical reflection on what is taking place, what is taking place morally when the country is moving in such a direction. That is a valid question for church officials to ask. I believe it is a valid question that church people should ask the legislators of the country. When the Bishops produced their statement and made it public, they started with two principles. As far as I know these two principles have not been accepted by many Members of the House as yet. First, the church, in directing how morality should be applied in an economy, should make sure that the particular group looking after the people should give a preferential option to the poor. Labour, labourers and workers should be above profit and capital. Those are two profound statements and two principles that will affect judgments surrounding anything that is done in our House as it relates to the economy of this nation.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to address my remarks to the amendment before us, particularly to suggest some reasons the Government might be well advised to support the amendment. In other words, we must ask what the committee will discuss.
Here are some ideas which might be of use to Hon. Members opposite. First, I think the whole world would accept the fact that many countries are in serious trouble, including Canada, because we have been spending more than we can

February 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
afford. It is a simple fact and there is no question about it. However, what will we do about it? We have come to a point now at which the Government is suddenly asking the people of Canada to agree to increased borrowing of $19 billion so that it can look after expenses it foresees in the next three or four months. The danger is obvious. Interest rates have barely started moving downward in the past six or seven months. If a $19 billion load is suddenly thrown on the people of Canada, it would cause interest rates to rise again, which is the basic cause of inflation. In the interest of the people of Canada, and the whole world for that matter, I hope that the Government allows time so that ordinary laymen may put forward a few common sense suggestions which might alleviate our concerns.
Just as a teaser, I will put forward one or two suggestions. First, three years ago, in the Standing Committee on Finance, which was dealing with interest rates, an idea was presented that if the Government were to continue borrowing, then the high interest rates which the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance were requesting should not be allowed, and that there should be new and innovative ideas with regard to borrowing which might appeal to a large section of the Canadian public. I will just state these as thoughts to be considered on their merits by the ordinary layman speaking quietly in committee. I would like to hear reactions from the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.
The Committee of which I spoke, having been set up three years ago, was cut off after the election in the spring of 1980, and the Government has refused to set up any similar committee since then. We will face the awful decision of destroying our little chance of survival if we do not consider this simple idea: if a Government bond is to be issued, why should it not be issued at a rate according to the value of money, or about 3 per cent? A rider could be attached to ensure an indexing of the rate and to ensure that the principal would be indexed at the end of each year based on inflation. Then purchasers would be guaranteed true returns on their investments. Several hundred thousand Canadians who buy bonds primarily for security might realize that this is a technique to stop inflation from rising too fast and also to reduce the demand on people for taxes now and in the future. It might also keep interest rates down, which is our biggest worry across the country as we try to get on our feet again. That is a simple suggestion and it should be considered. I do not expect that $19 billion would be coming forward in this particular offer. As I mentioned, such a proposal was accepted.
Why should we not consider another proposal? We should compare our charts with what the Americans have been doing since last July. The Americans are not making any big fuss about borrowing money. They are quietly doing what the Bank of Canada Act allows us to do here, but we are not doing it. If we compare the figures of a year ago with those of today, we find that the money supply is the same. However, the American money supply has been rising steadily since last July. Of course, there is the odd dip in the weekly accounts, but, generally speaking, the Americans have decided to use the money supply approach instead of borrowing. It will work to reduce inflation as long as there is an unused labour supply, unused plant capacity and slow circulation of money. Those
are the three elements. I think that in the quietness of committee, we might be able to persuade the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance officials to consider this alternative, rather than frightening the daylights out of the entire country with a $19 billion request for money in the next four or five months.
The two ideas I just mentioned are based on ideas put forward in the Standing Committee in 1979. For evidence of the effect of a standing committee of the House, one should consider the interest rate charts of the Bank of Canada. One would find that the minute such a committee was appointed and began to ask questions of the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance, the interest rate stopped rising, and that was true throughout a four-month period. The minute a new Government was formed which refused to let the Committee continue sitting, the interest rates fell, and then rose to a record high. I am suggesting that if a such committee were sitting, it would have a much more salutory effect on the Bank of Canada and Department of Finance officials than anything we could do.
I want to conclude by simply pointing out that now is the time to reconsider. We faced the same problem 25 years ago in Parliament. The difficulties were not nearly as immense as today. We set up a Royal Commission under the chairmanship of Dana Porter, which reported in 1964. This Royal Commission's Report has sat idle on the shelves of the Government ever since. I have asked several questions about this Report over the years and have had no response. Our starting place in that committee would be to read this Report which is sensible, common sense and has many ideas that could slowly speed up our exit from the deep recession in which we find ourselves.

Mr. Speaker, a few years ago the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that he had "wrestled inflation to the ground." Unfortunately, I guess he has never made a statement that was more misleading than that, because since that period of time we have seen one of the most inflationary periods in Canadian history. I guess a decision has to be made which comes first, inflation or high interest rates. Inflation causes high interest rates; interest rates cause inflation. And just like the chicken and the egg, which comes first? Actually, we have to realize that the Government is really the only body in Canada that can do anything about either one. Businesses and Canadian citizens can all work away at it, but unless the Government establishes the climate, there is no way that we can keep either one down or keep either one in place.
I well remember, before I came into the House of Commons, that I was told then that if ever the period arrived when the inflation factor was over 4 per cent, the country was going to be in serious difficulty. Here we are a number of years later, and the inflation rate is well over 4 per cent. If we could get the inflation factor down to 4 per cent, we would be doing well.
February 28, 1983

There is absolutely no way that we are ever going to get inflation down with the present Government policies. We should realize that the last number of years have been really good years in the Canadian economy, better than perhaps we have ever experienced, and yet our national debt has increased more during that period of time than it ever has before in Canadian history. The debt cost today is considerably greater, one and one half times greater, than the budget was when the present Prime Minister took office. So this should really tell Canadians what is happening.
Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada made a statement that I agree with, that those people who invest money have a right to have a return on it, and if the interest rate is not over the inflationary factor then they are not getting any return on their investment. Therefore it is of paramount importance that inflation be held down as well as interest rates because of the fact that interest rates will kill us. The person who is investing money would be just as well off if we had an inflation factor of, say, 1 or 2 per cent, and he was getting 5 per cent on his money. He would probably make a greater return on his money in that kind of situation than he is at the present time.
I believe that at the present time the number one villain in Canada is high interest rates. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has just told the House what effect high interest rates have on our Canadian way of life. For instance, when we have a Government that is exceeding its expenditures this year and will have to borrow money, probably $30 billion, $35 billion or $40 billion next year just to operate, and if it makes the same mistake next year that it made this year, then certainly we will have a deficit in the $40 billion bracket.
Mr. Speaker, you will remember that this year when we started out we were going to have a $10.6 billion deficit, then it got to $17 billion, then up to $23 billion, then to $26 or $27 billion, and it could well be up to $30 billion before we are through. So if we miss it by $20 billion next year, it means that we are at $50 billion, because the Government now says that it will need to have a $30 billion deficit next year.
This is why we are in such serious times. The role that the Bank of Canada plays in establishing the weekly Thursday prime rate is not the only influence that the Government has on interest rates. As I said, its deficit spending and its massive borrowing is creating a situation whereby too many Governments, corporations and individuals are chasing the too few dollars that are up for borrowing. The end result is that this competition in the borrowing market forces interest rates to spiral upwards. The results of high interest rates have been devastating for Canadians, for small businesses, for farmers, for consumers and for home owners.
There are farmers who do not know how they are going to be able to finance putting their crops in the ground this spring. That is a very, very serious situation that the Government has done nothing whatsoever to face. Countless thousands of Canadians have lost their homes or have forestalled the purchasing of a new or older home because of the unpredictability of interest rates. Thousands of small businesses and
Borrowing Authority
individuals have been forced into bankruptcy; and unknown thousands of others have simply closed the door and walked away. These victims are not reported in the bankruptcy statistics but, if they were, the totals would be considerably higher.
This present Government has no idea of exactly how much money it owes. The gross debt is estimated at about $140 billion. Crown corporation debt is another $55 billion. In addition, the Government is using, to meet current spending obligations, the almost $50 billion that public servants, RCMP and Armed Forces have contributed to their pension plans. Simple arithmetic tells us that these three areas total almost $250 billion in liabilities.
I have said on other occasions that the Government should not be administering the pension funds of civil servants, RCMP and Armed Forces personel. These funds should be removed entirely from the general revenues of the Government and placed in the hands of trustees who will ensure that the funds are administrated wisely and well. I cite as examples of good trusteeship some of the pension plans in the private sector where these funds are invested in blue chip investments which bring handsome returns, and at the same time generate some economic activity in the community and in the nation. This is not a new solution to a problem. This is just the practical application of common sense. For years the Government paid a pitance in interest to these pension contributions, 4 per cent per annum. It is considerably higher now but still far less than these massive pools of capital could earn in the marketplace, invested wisely by trustees.
I said earlier that the Government really does not know how much it owes. Can any Member on the Treasury benches tell me what the Government's obligations are in contingent liabilities? Can any Member on the Treasury benches tell me what long-term low-interest loans to other nations, some of them hostile to our way of life, are costing Canadians? Can any Government Minister tell me the Government's response to the Auditor General's charge that about $4 billion of these loans ought to be written off and considered as gifts or outright grants? Our spending is out of control. The Auditor General has told us that, and we have no reason to believe that the Government has been able to bring it under control.
We have a foreign aid bill in the ballpark of $2 billion. One million dollars is dispersed in multilateral aid through the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the United Nations and so on. The other $1 billion is parcelled out in bilateral aid by CIDA, which has almost 1,100 employees in red brick skyscrapers in Hull, and about 55 people out in the field. I ask you, how can one administer a foreign aid program effectively sitting on you-know-what over in Hull? Better that we should funnel these funds through the churches, the Unitarian Services, the Red Cross, rather than just letting them trickle down through CIDA programs.
I would like to go on, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I will do so at a later stage in the debate.

The unemployed workers have published a scathing attack on job-creating programs, an attack I would like to go into in some detail. It reflects many of the problems that I have had as a Member of Parliament in trying to deal with those programs to see that the people are paid on time and have access to the program.
The union is frustrated by its inability to get help and protection from the job-creation programs, with the kind of job-creation approach this Liberal Government is taking. We do not see that this $19 billion will improve that situation in Canada.
The Organization of Unemployed Workers asked certain things in this brief. They are asking to continue being represented by the union from which they are laid off so that they
February 28, 1983

can have some protection under the job-creation programs and can find jobs which they are prepared and willing to take. They are asking for some expansion of public sector employment opportunities through meaningful work projects within the community which will give well-paid, meaningful, longterm employment opportunities.
They are asking for the industry to participate in funding some projects that they are responsible for, particularly in the forest industry. Why should Government come along with job-creation programs to support the corporate sector, which is quite willing to lay off more and more people each year with the excuse in its rationalization that it is making us competitive? Basically what it is doing is making them competitive and throwing Canadians out of work.
I have a petition from the Organization of Unemployed Workers which I will table in the House tomorrow when petitions are called. Because of the frustration that this organization is feeling, representing as it does the work force in Port Alberni, it is calling for unemployment insurance benefits to be extended, not because these people are particularly interested in staying on unemployment, but they have seen the failure of job-creation and the failure of the federal Government to deal with unemployment in a meaningful way. They want unemployment insurance benefits to be increased to 90 per cent of their insurable level so that they can maintain their homes and families. The job-creation program is becoming more and more of an obvious failure. The budget we are expecting to be brought down and the $19 billion we are being asked to approve had better deal with the problems of the workers in this country.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-ROLE OF ALASTAIR GILLESPIE. (B) USE OF FUNDS ALLOCATED TO NOVA SCOTIA
THE ADMINISTRATION-ROLE OF ALASTAIR GILLESPIE. (B) USE OF FUNDS ALLOCATED TO NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue on the theme of the questions which I asked the Minister of Energy (Mr. Chretien) last Thursday, and to elaborate a little concerning the overt attempts, in my view, by officials to circumvent the Parliamentary guidelines of good behaviour in order to provide an artificial legitimacy for the payments to be made to Alastair Gillespie and Associates in this project.
The Minister, upon reflection, Mr. Speaker, should realize that these efforts only serve to implicate the Government more deeply in the special treatment, access and favouritism, or whatever you want to call it, towards a former Cabinet colleague in relation to this Nova Scotia energy project. Indeed,
Adjournment Debate
the oil substitution agreement itself, as part of the National Energy Program, was stretched in order to accommodate that kind of project which Alastair Gillespie espoused. When efforts were made to alter the submission to Treasury Board, the guidelines were not being followed, they were being circumvented in advance. Anyone looking at this situation, without extreme prejudice, can see this very clearly.
The people of Cape Breton and of Nova Scotia are sick and tired, Mr. Speaker, of being the victims of rhetoric and job proposals by a series of Liberal Cabinet Ministers and the former defeated Premier. A quick review of Liberal promises to Cape Breton reveals that the defeated Premier of Nova Scotia, now Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) traded for years on the promises that they were going to build a new steel mill at Gabarouse, or to use the argot of the industry, a Greenfields project. After milking this for all the political capital it was worth, they forgot about it.
They also raised people's hopes in Cape Breton with another energy-related project, the celebrated Shaheen oil refinery. Land was expropriated at enormous cost but nothing happened here, either.
The most recent piece of "puffery" from the Deputy Prime Minister was his announcement that a large steel fabricating facility was being considered for the port Hawkesbury area, which would supply 1,000 jobs. When questioned by reporters for more details, and after it was pointed out to him that such a plant was already available in nearby Pictou County in my constituency, where over 1,000 people also needed work in an existing plant, the Deputy Prime Minister, said in his usual obfuscatory manner, "Well, it is only a concept". Some concept, Mr. Speaker. Some track record.
The persistent raising of the hopes and aspirations of the people of Cape Breton by the Liberals, while shirking their responsibility to produce something practical, is costing them their political credibility there. I am sure that recent private polls have driven that home to them very, very forcibly.
Recent international pricing developments, as well, regarding petroleum products, are now showing the people of Nova Scotia and, indeed, of Canada, how bankrupt and ill advised the federal Government's National Energy Program really is. The revelations about the liquefaction of coal and the details of this project are just other examples of the latest Liberal blunder. The Province of Nova Scotia, naturally, was anxious to participate in this pilot project, but, as usual, the primary funding, the concept, the impetus, and much of the gain, was designed by the Liberals to benefit themselves. Surely, the Cabinet documents indicate that knowledgeable officials in the Department of Energy knew from the start that this project had little chance of bringing any practical benefits to the people of Cape Breton.
The former defeated Premier of Nova Scotia, incidentally, living up to his nickname of "Gabby", intervened the other day in the House and asked a question designed to provoke me. He asked the question of his colleague, the Hon. Member for

February 28, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey). I would like to say at this time by way of a riposte that I could remind him of the details involving a "page" from his past, and a well-known trip he made to Toronto to secure legal advice when he was Premier of Nova Scotia from a prominent Toronto lawyer in order to discourage a reporter who was interested in the incident. And later on, if I recall, a similar intervention was made with the CBC to forestall another fascinating piece of research. However, I am always willing to elaborate on any detail or questions involving my conduct, both public and private. If the former Premier wishes to elaborate on this, I am sure that people would be interested.
However, as the late John Diefenbaker used to say, when you are after big game, you should not be diverted by rabbits. I want to go back to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and point out that he and his predecessors, both of whom have had legal training, must realize upon mature reflection what a clumsy subterfuge this attempt was to avoid the very proper intent of Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) guidelines to regulate the conduct of this Parliament. He must be given credit for that. Both of them would gain in stature if they would simply admit this.
Speaking in the House last Thursday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made a point of referring to the sacrifices that a former Cabinet minister makes in public life. As he put it so colloquially, they should not have to go to the Sparks Street Mall with a cup in order to earn a living. I think it is a fair comment that neither the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources nor his predecessor could have gained any more out of life in the private sector than they did by coming into public service. I venture to say that instead of making sacrifices, they are the net beneficiaries, as many of us are, of entering public life. To cry poor mouth after having served the country under these circumstances is a pretty artificial way of gaining sympathy.
While on the subject of the private sector, I must say that it is strange indeed that Mr. Gillespie, apparently a knowledgeable businessman with a lot of versatility, chose his own department and his own deputy minister to pursue his business initiatives. One would have thought he would have pursued some of the other myriad and imaginative ways there are of making money.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-ROLE OF ALASTAIR GILLESPIE. (B) USE OF FUNDS ALLOCATED TO NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has taken issue with some of the answers provided him. I certainly wish to take issue with some of the comments he has made today. In particular, he made reference to things the officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources had done in terms of circumventing guidelines established by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I wish to refute all the arguments made by the Hon. Member for Central Nova and point out to him that the money contained in the Canada-Nova Scotia agreement of 1977, $9.2
million, was provided to a bank account in Halifax, and was to be administered independently by two individuals representing the Government of Canada and two individuals representing the Province of Nova Scotia. An independent joint management committee was administering the money.
It is sad that the Hon. Member for Central Nova dismisses, as the interim Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) has, the benefits of such a project to industrial Cape Breton. Aside from the 2,000 or 2,500 jobs that might be created in the coal mines, there is the economic multiplier of three or four which brings it up to 7,000 or 8,000 jobs. As he ought to know that that is very important in industrial Cape Breton.
Notwithstanding the jobs, there is the issue of self-sufficiency. That 40,000 to 60,000 barrels of oil per day is being displaced is not a serious thing in the Canadian context, but when you look at it from a Nova Scotia perspective it is great indeed.
It ought to be noted that when the Hon. Member for Central Nova was minister of Regional and Economic Expansion in the former Government, he did not provide any money to help the Donkin mine proceed. When Sysco came looking for financial assistance from the federal Government, what money did he provide for the people of Cape Breton? Not one cent. He was a Conservative minister, dealing with a Conservative Government in Nova Scotia. What deal did he get for the coal miners of Cape Breton on the price of coal sold to the Nova Scotia Power Corporation? He got nothing. He has got nothing for them for a good many years, not only while he was a minister, but while he has been a Member of Parliament. Where has he been for 22 months while this issue has been going on? Where has the Hon. Member for Nova Scotia been-asleep?

subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-IMPORTATION OF PORNOGRAPHIC VIDEO CASSETTES. (B) APPLICATION OF TAX WRITE-OFFS- REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE AMENDED
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-IMPORTATION OF PORNOGRAPHIC VIDEO CASSETTES. (B) APPLICATION OF TAX WRITE-OFFS- REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE AMENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 14, I rose in the House to ask a question concerning the importation of pornographic material into Canada, and I was not satisfied with the answer I obtained from the Minister.
I should like to point out that the advent of mass access to video cassette players has opened the floodgates for pornography in Canada. Since the introduction of the home video cassette recorder in 1975, the video equipment market has expanded by at least 300 per cent. One can only guess the effects this has had on the pornography industry in Canada.
Recent estimates of the dollar value of the industry in North America range from a low of $1 billion, according to The Globe and Mail of last July 6, to a high of $50 billion per annum, as given by a spokesman of the special anti-pornography squad of the Ontario Provincial Police. This is one of the few police forces in Canada which has a special squad to handle pornography. I think it is very commendable.
February 28, 1983

It has been estimated that 65 per cent of the American film industry is now engaged in the production of pornography. Public outrage at the exploitive nature of pornographic material being distributed has risen at a comparable rate. The demonstrations against the Red Hot Video outlets in Vancouver indicate the depth of this public anger. While the illegality of the fire-bombing of some of these outlets must be condemned, we must not ignore the frustration felt by the public with the inactivity of various levels of Government and their paralytic inability to control the growth of this industry.
Many people question why we should in fact control the growth of pornography in Canada. The answer to this is very simple. Films, magazines and other media have a powerful effect on the formation of public attitudes and morals. If people regularly see the depiction of immoral behaviour on television, or in other forms, they will soon take this to be the norm and, therefore, acceptable.
According to the present obscenity section of the Criminal Code, obscenity is judged "according to contemporary community standards". This leads to a Catch 22 situation where community standards are continually dropping as more pornographic material is introduced. It all amounts to a gradual but relentless erosion of public morals.
While it does not appear to be the duty of Government to set down a strict moral code which all citizens must follow, as in present day Iran, it is the responsibility of Government to protect the potential victims of such exploitive material. In this sense I am concerned in particular about women and children who are portrayed in material which is not only sexually exploitive but also contains acts of violence in conjunction with gratuitous sex. Obviously "kiddy porn" and violent pornography involving such acts as rape are clearly unacceptable to society at large and, equally clear, it is the duty of Government to control the malignant spread of such destructive material.
At this stage the Government is failing dismally in controlling the growth of the pornography industry in Canada; 95 per cent of all pornography is imported from the United States. Only about 5 per cent of these imports are intercepted at the border. Most commonly, once one video cassette is smuggled into the country, copies are made at either licit or elicit dubbing houses, and the resulting cassettes are distributed to retailers and/or consumers.
Because of the slight possibility of actually being caught and prosecuted, the distribution of these cassettes is a low-risk, high-profit investment. There can be little doubt that organized crime has entered into this lucrative business.
In reply to my question in the House on February 14, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) acknowledged that his Department had been less than effective in stemming this growing flood of pornographic material into the country, and indicated that the "Customs and Excise division, took action in this area and banned the entry of cassettes considered by a large majority of Canadians to be immoral". This is simply not good enough. When only one cassette in 20 is intercepted at the border, and when each cassette that gets through customs can be so easily copied, then the Department, and more specifically the Minister, must do more than simply
Adjournment Debate
ban the entry of offensive material. He must take action to enforce that ban.
In fact, not only are the efforts of the Department of National Revenue inadequate and ineffective, but the current income tax structure could actually encourage the establishment of a domestic pornography industry, up until now something we have been able to avoid. Because the generous tax write-off provision for films produced in Canada does not differentiate between pornographic and non-pornographic material, some domestic producers could enter the field and could in fact use the resulting films as part of their Canadian content quota in order to satisfy CRTC regulations. Instead of inadvertently encouraging the establishment of a domestic pornography industry by incentives such as these, we should be ensuring that there is no domestic production at all, as well as addressing the difficult task of eliminating the importation of pornographic material.
I realize that it may be well nigh impossible to prevent the importation of "hard core" pornography. However, I think that the Government should at least make a highly visible effort to control its importation to stem the tide. In the area of smuggling of illegal drugs, we commonly use undercover agents and are able to make large drug "busts" that are a very visible disincentive to drug traffickers. We should be able to mount similar operations to discourage those who import pornography, and set an example by our treatment of those who are caught. Good long prison sentences and heavy fines for those convicted of smuggling pornography would be a clear deterrent to importers, and would thereby make this trade much less attractive. We must demonstrate the resolve of the Government to stop, or at least curtail this immoral and exploitive trade. That is what the Government has so far failed to demonstrate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-IMPORTATION OF PORNOGRAPHIC VIDEO CASSETTES. (B) APPLICATION OF TAX WRITE-OFFS- REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE AMENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as noted in the Minister of National Revenue's (Mr. Bussieres) response in the House on February 14 concerning this issue, the Department is taking all necessary measures to enforce the laws of the country as strictly as possible. I am sure the Hon. Member realizes that, in the case of articles such as video cassettes where the contents are not immediately apparent to a cursory examination, the costs involved in making a detailed examination of every importation would be prohibitive. The Department is aware that some importers are attempting to import material by clandestine means to escape detection, and it is taking all possible action to apprehend this material at a reasonable cost to the taxpayer and with a minimum of disruption to legitimate importers.
In this respect, the Department conducts spot checks on a sample basis of importations of this type of material, as well as examination of any material of a suspicious nature. The Department also conducts examinations on the basis of information provided by law enforcement agencies or other sources.

February 28, 1983
Adjournment Debate
If the Department were to attempt to conduct detailed examinations of all importations of video cassettes, video tapes, films, video games or similar articles, several hundred additional customs officers would be required across the country.
With respect to the taxation side of the matter, I must advise that where a film is acquired by a taxpayer for the purpose of gaining income therefrom, the Income Tax Act and regulations provide for a claim of capital cost allowance at the rate of 100 per cent of the cost, if the film is a certified feature production or a certified short production, and 30 per cent of the cost of other films.
Certification is mainly to the effect that a film has the required Canadian economic content, and this determination is the responsibility of the Department of Communications. At this stage the subject matter would become evident, and if it appeared to be pornographic the advice of the Department of Justice could be sought. Revenue Canada's responsibility is to apply the Income Tax Act and regulations as enacted. The Department of Finance is responsible for proposing amendments to the Income Tax Act and regulations.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-RESCHEDULING OF LOANS TOSMALL BUSINESSES AND FARMERS
BANKS AND BANKING-RESCHEDULING OF LOANS TOSMALL BUSINESSES AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any Member of Parliament who is fortunate enough to represent an agricultural constituency of Canada, or has an agricultural component in his or her constituency will be well aware of the incredible pressures that food producers are under these days. Whether one is talking about a cattle, hog or sheep operation, or poultry farms, market gardening or wheat farming-no matter what the situation-by and large, the agricultural sector in this country is experiencing pressure unprecedented since the 1930s.
Back in the 1930s, various provincial Governments, using the legislation available to them, passed legislation to provide the much needed relief to this sector. While it was a pittance, it was accepted by those in receipt as at least a gesture of good faith. It eventually became necessary for the federal Government to change it. In 1934, the Government of Canada introduced the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934. That Act enabled pressure to be brought to bear on various lending institutions to assist the farmers of Canada to stay on their land.
I want to take a few moments to read from Bill C-653, which is before the House. It is an Act to revive the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. It reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to revive the moribund provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which provide a simple and inexpensive procedure for farmers to rearrange their affairs when cash flow becomes insufficient to meet current obligations as they come due.
The Act as framed is only applicable where two-thirds of a farmer's indebtedness was incurred before May 1935. In addition, the Act, originally general in its application, was subsequently narrowed to cover only the Provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Bill would remove both of these limitations.
In my estimation, the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson), at a time when the issue of farm bankruptcies was being raised day after day in the House, is a gesture, at least on behalf of the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, that there are actions and steps that could be taken by the Government in an effort to bring some semblance of security to the hardpressed farming community. It is well known right now, for example, what the banks are doing to many farmers, ranchers and food producers generally in our country.
In western Canada it is not now uncommon for the banks to go to the food producers and tell them that they will not have their traditional working capital advance unless they sell off portions of their property or operation. This means there is a flood of property, equipment and land on the market especially, in western Canada and, I suspect, in other parts of Canada as well. I speak of western Canada since I am a representative from that area and am more familiar with it.
As a result, land and property values, along with equipment values are being depressed. This brings hardship to bear on all food producers of that region. It also causes hardship to equipment dealers who are now faced with the dumping of equipment on the market. The result is a downward migration of property values and the validity of farming operations, simply because the banks are bringing this undue pressure to bear in an attempt to maintain their own cash flows.
I believe we now have a situation in which the long term viability and profits of the banks must be considered in relation to the long term credibility of Canada's food producers. I would be the first to admit that both are important, but it is not an issue of one or the other. We have just received annual reports of various banks in Canada which indicate healthy profit returns which, while not excessive, are up to $300 million.
As Members of Parliament we are all aware of the number of bankruptcies being faced by food producers in this country, let alone those myriads of food producers who are simply forced to walk away from their hopes, dreams, and the ability to create a fundamental aspect of Canadian life.
Normally one would go on and simply identify the critical nature of the situation, and those areas where the Government has refused to act. I am not able to do that today, because the Government has taken the first step toward solving this very critical problem. It has introduced, through the personage of Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex Bill C-653, which would essentially resolve the situation, in the short term. It would allow food producers to stay on the land and continue producing food. It would adjust their financial affairs through a quasi-judicial process, enabling this most critical sector of our economy to continue.
I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) during a recent Question Period, why not bring this Bill forward? I am certain that Members of the Opposition would allow passage of the Bill without debate, because of the important role it
February 28, 1983

would play. It would be a simple matter for the Government to bring the Bill from first reading to second reading. We will put it through all stages of the House with perhaps no debate at all. We could deal with it in an afternoon, because I do not think a single Member of the House does not appreciate the seriousness of this matter. I encourage the Government to take this necessary step, and introduce this critical legislation as quickly as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-RESCHEDULING OF LOANS TOSMALL BUSINESSES AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us are very deeply concerned about the effects of high interest rates, and the practice being followed, not only by the banks, but also by lending institutions, in scheduling debt, or in asking businessmen and farmers to repay their debts. I myself raised the issue with the Canadian Banker's Association during the pre-budget consultation held with them in December. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) also raised this matter with them at that time, as well as on previous occasions.
The banks have shown considerable concern about keeping businessmen and farmers afloat during this difficult period. I think the real, overall cure to this huge problem is to ensure that interest rates in general come down. We have heard some good news along that line recently, as I am sure the Hon. Member would agree. This week prime rates were at 11.25 per cent; one year mortgage rates were at 11.75 per cent; and our official Bank of Canada rate was at 9.48 per cent. This is possibly because our inflation rate is coming down. Prices actually fell instead of rising in December and January. That was the first time, in a long time, we had seen that phenomenon. Our annualized 12 month rate, from January to January,
Adjournment Debate
is 8.3 per cent, and our six month rate, from June to January, is 6 per cent.
American rates are also dropping. This week, six major American banks announced primes of 10.5 per cent. These are the key indicators to our people that relief is coming.
We have our own house in order. We are beginning to bring under control the forces which push interest rates up. We are allowing ourselves room, within our own economy, to benefit from foreign improvements, such as the drop in the United States prime rate. However, we are still concerned about specific individuals while this is taking place.
The previous Minister of Finance set up a special system to review complaints about interest rates from businessmen and farmers. In answer to the Hon. Member the other day, the current Minister of Finance made a pledge that he would take specific cases to the banks, as well as to the Inspector General for Banks, asking them to review these harsh circumstances once again. The Minister raised tl^e question of the Private Members' Bill of the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson). We have taken note of it, and have started to act on this side to give both personal and general attention to the whole question of interest rates. We have a system in place to take care of individuals, and we have a general attack on the underlying causes of high interest rates.
